title: The explanation and the cost
lines: Calling an exhausting shift flexible does not give the worker back their night.
Holding the Dirty Thing by the Clean Side asks who pays for respectable explanations.
Its distinctive test follows the burden, even when an institution serves a real purpose.
The book connects public authority, emotional resilience, and algorithmic decisions through that question.
It asks readers to separate necessary cooperation from costs made difficult to challenge.

title: Who receives the night
lines: Imagine a bakery calling its new night rota an efficiency improvement.
Bread still needs to reach the shop each morning.
But the same baker now carries more of the disrupted sleep.
Management's label cannot tell us whether that distribution is necessary.
The book's burden test asks who benefits, who bears costs, and who can object.
Some constraints are real; their current allocation still needs justification.

title: Calm is not a correction
lines: The emotional chapters ask what happens when resilience replaces a response to exhaustion.
Support can help someone face pressure without making that pressure acceptable.
In our example, a calmer conversation leaves the night rota unchanged.
AI could intensify this distance when a score appears to make the decision.
The book also asks whether automation could remove some degrading work instead.
